title: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree, where every node's value is greater than all values in its left subtree and less than all values in its right subtree.
shortTitle: Validate Binary Search Tree — in-range DFS with min/max bounds

s1_definition.profdef: Validating a binary search tree checks that every node obeys the ordering invariant across its entire subtree, not just its immediate children. The robust solution is a depth-first recursion that carries a lower and upper bound; each node must lie strictly within its bounds, and as you descend you tighten the bounds, passing the current value as the new upper bound to the left and the new lower bound to the right.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh organizes account records in a tree so searches are fast, with smaller account numbers to the left and larger to the right. To verify the tree is correctly ordered, he checks each record against an allowed range. Starting with no limits, as he goes left the numbers must all stay below the parent, and as he goes right they must all stay above it. If any record falls outside the range inherited from its ancestors, the ordering is broken.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every node must lie strictly between a lower and upper bound inherited from its ancestors, and those bounds tighten as you descend left and right.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Validating a binary search tree checks that every node obeys the ordering invariant across its entire subtree, not just its immediate children. The robust solution is a depth-first recursion that carries a lower and upper bound; each node must lie strictly within its bounds, and as you descend you tighten the bounds, passing the current value as the new upper bound to the left and the new lower bound to the right.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh organizes account records in a tree so searches are fast, with smaller account numbers to the left and larger to the right. To verify the tree is correctly ordered, he checks each record against an allowed range. Starting with no limits, as he goes left the numbers must all stay below the parent, and as he goes right they must all stay above it. If any record falls outside the range inherited from its ancestors, the ordering is broken.

**One line to remember:** Every node must lie strictly between a lower and upper bound inherited from its ancestors, and those bounds tighten as you descend left and right.

sections.s2_technical:
The common mistake is checking only that a node is greater than its left child and less than its right child. That is insufficient, because the invariant applies to the whole subtree: a node deep in the left subtree can violate an ancestor's bound even while satisfying its immediate parent. The correct approach threads a valid open interval down the recursion.

Each call receives the node plus a lower and upper bound. The node's value must be strictly greater than the lower bound and strictly less than the upper bound. For example: `if (value <= low || value >= high) return false;`.

When you recurse left, the current node becomes the new upper bound, because everything to the left must be smaller. For example: `validate(node.left, low, value)`. When you recurse right, the current node becomes the new lower bound. For example: `validate(node.right, value, high)`.

The initial bounds are negative and positive infinity, so the root is unconstrained. Using boxed types or `Long` sentinels avoids edge cases at the integer extremes. For example: `validate(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE)`.

The time complexity is linear because each node is checked once, and the space is proportional to the height from the recursion stack. A senior nuance is the elegant alternative: an inorder traversal of a valid binary search tree yields strictly increasing values, so you can validate by checking that each inorder-visited value exceeds the previous one. Both approaches are linear; the bounds approach fails fast on the first violation, while the inorder approach is a clean one-pass check and naturally handles the strict-increase requirement.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, account records are indexed in a binary search tree by account number for fast lookup. After a bulk insert, the operations team must verify the tree is still a valid search tree, because a single misplaced record silently breaks every future lookup. This is exactly how Validate Binary Search Tree works — it confirms the global ordering invariant.

Problem 2 — A record deep in a subtree could satisfy its immediate parent yet violate an ancestor's bound, which a naive neighbor check would miss. This is exactly why the validation threads inherited min and max bounds down the recursion.

The mini-project builds an `AccountNode` class keyed by account number, a `BstValidatorService` with a bounds-based recursive validate and logging, and a runnable demo that checks a valid tree and an invalid one.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the valid tree rooted at 5000.

Step 1: Validate 5000 with bounds negative infinity and positive infinity. 5000 is within range. Recurse left with upper bound 5000 and right with lower bound 5000.

Step 2: Validate 3000 with bounds negative infinity and 5000. 3000 is within range. Recurse left with upper bound 3000 and right with bounds 3000 and 5000.

Step 3: Validate 1000 with bounds negative infinity and 3000. In range, children null, returns true. Validate 4000 with bounds 3000 and 5000. In range, children null, returns true. So 3000's subtree is valid.

Step 4: Validate 8000 with bounds 5000 and positive infinity. In range. Recurse left with bounds 5000 and 8000.

Step 5: Validate 7000 with bounds 5000 and 8000. In range, children null, returns true. So 8000's subtree is valid, and the whole tree returns true.

Step 6: For the invalid tree, validation reaches 4500 as the left child of 8000. The inherited bounds are lower 5000 and upper 8000, because everything in 8000's subtree must exceed the ancestor 5000. 4500 is not greater than the lower bound 5000, so it returns false and the whole validation short-circuits to invalid, even though 4500 is correctly less than its immediate parent 8000.

```text
2026-10-26T18:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Account Index BST Validation
2026-10-26T18:20:00Z [INFO] Account index is a VALID BST — lookups safe
2026-10-26T18:20:00Z [SEVERE] Account index is INVALID — misplaced record, lookups unsafe
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  validate(5000, -inf, +inf)         ✓
    ├─ left  validate(3000, -inf, 5000)   ✓
    │    ├─ validate(1000, -inf, 3000)    ✓
    │    └─ validate(4000, 3000, 5000)    ✓
    └─ right validate(8000, 5000, +inf)   ✓
         └─ validate(7000, 5000, 8000)    ✓
  → VALID

  Invalid case:
  validate(8000, 5000, +inf) ✓
    └─ left validate(4500, 5000, 8000)
         4500 <= low(5000) → FALSE (violates ANCESTOR bound)
  → INVALID (naive parent check would have passed it!)
```

```text
  │  - validate(node, low, high): boolean │ strict open interval
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Descent rule:
    left  → (low, node.value)   value becomes new upper bound
    right → (node.value, high)  value becomes new lower bound
  Use Long.MIN/MAX sentinels to avoid integer-edge bugs.

  Contract: true iff global BST invariant holds at every node.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Validating a binary search tree is a problem where the obvious solution is wrong, and interviewers know it. The naive approach checks only that each node is greater than its left child and less than its right child, but the binary search tree invariant is global: every node must be greater than everything in its left subtree and less than everything in its right subtree, across the entire subtree, not just the immediate neighbors. A node deep in a subtree can satisfy its parent yet violate an ancestor.

My robust solution threads a valid open interval down the recursion. Each node receives a lower and upper bound and must lie strictly between them. When I recurse left, the current value becomes the new upper bound because everything to the left must be smaller, and when I recurse right, the current value becomes the new lower bound. I start the root with negative and positive infinity, and I use Long sentinels so values at the integer extremes do not cause false failures.

The complexity is linear with space proportional to the height. I always mention the elegant alternative: an inorder traversal of a valid binary search tree yields strictly increasing values, so I can validate by confirming each inorder value exceeds the previous one. Both are linear; the bounds approach fails fast on the first violation, while the inorder approach is a clean single pass.

In my project at National Bank of India, account records are indexed in a binary search tree by account number for fast lookup, and after a bulk insert we must verify the tree is still valid. A single misplaced record silently breaks every future lookup, and the bounds-based validation catches exactly the dangerous case where a record satisfies its immediate parent but violates an ancestor's range, which a naive neighbor check would have passed.
